newsitem.title: USA: Dollar needs big Fed hike for heft - U.S. experts.
newsitem.headline: Dollar needs big Fed hike for heft - U.S. experts.

text.p: A slim majority of economists expects the Federal Reserve to raise official interest rates by 25 basis points on Tuesday, but foreign exchange experts said the dollar will need more aggressive rate action to bolster its fundamental outlook.

The dollar is currently discounting a 25-basis point tightening in the 5.25 percent federal funds target rate. It may take a bigger hike or an increase in the discount rate, as sought by regional Fed banks, to give the dollar an added lift, experts said.

"Fifty (basis points) would probably be enough to push the dollar through the top of the technical trading range," said John Nelson, senior vice president of foreign exchage trading at ABN-AMRO Bank. "But I think an interest rate hike of 25 points is definitely priced in and 50 is probably partially priced."

Seventeen of 30 economists in the latest Reuters poll said the Fed is likely to raise short-term interest rates at its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting next week. All but one of the 17 predicted a 25-basis point rate hike.

The poll followed news this week that eight of 12 district Fed banks are pushing for a higher discount rate, which is currently set at 5.0 percent. But the results were largely unchanged from a September 6 poll in which 16 of 30 experts predicted higher rates.
If Fed policy makers do deliver a discount rate hike Tuesday, it might buttress the dollar by broadcasting a concern that festering wage pressures require a dose of stronger medicine.

"Meaning they are signaling more of a longer-term need for higher rates, the discount (rate) would have more of an impact than just a 25-basis point hike (in the federal funds target rate)," said Mark Gargano, manager of foreign exchange at First Union National Bank.
The Fed last adjusted interest rates on January 31, when it lowered the discount rate and fed funds rates by 25 basis points each.
The dollar has gyrated in the last week while market players became overloaded by myriad Fed action scenarios.
After low inflation and weak retail sales data buoyed bonds and depressed the dollar late last week, Tuesday's news about the regional Feds refueled bets on a credit tightening.
"It rekindled the expectations," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal in Chicago. "It

really does confirm ... the regional banks are far more hawkish on inflation than the Fed governors themselves. I'm not sure whether it is anything different from that, or whether they are laying the groundwork for something," he added.
Any U.S. rate hike is expected to boost the dollar more versus currencies in Europe, where rates are falling, rather than against the yen.
Japanese deposit rates are expected to remain stable in the foreseeable future, traders said.
"Rate spreads, in essence, should favor the U.S. because you've got European (rates) dropping and U.S.(rates) rising, so spreads should be widening dramatically," Gargano said.
However, the technical picture is more important than the interest rate outlook for the dollar right now, some traders said.
Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, agreed. "Whether the Fed moves 25 basis points or not is not, in the scheme of things, a bullish or bearish factor," he said.
But, Nelson added that "the absence of an interest rate hike would probably put the dollar under some pressure."
